what: the shape of the reference gradient itself: which KIND of parameter carries OpenFold3's gradient mass. Summed directly from bundle_min_043/grads_f64_043.pt on qb2 (4,170 tensors, 368,296,732 parameters, model squared norm 10.279642678524985). CPU only, no device opened.
basis: upstream OpenFold3 0.4.3, the revision this campaign claims. Not the 0.5.0 / 4,147 bundle.
headline: 84.6253 % of the model's squared gradient norm sits in 1-D tensors -- LayerNorm gains and biases -- that hold 0.0952 % of its parameters. 350,588 scalars out of 368,296,732 carry five sixths of the gradient. A parity claim about OpenFold3's gradient is, to first order, a claim about LayerNorm backward on the single track.
top_12_reading: ten of the twelve are LayerNorm gain/bias vectors on the single (s) track inside diffusion_module. Only two matrices appear at all, and the larger of them is 3.39 %.

the_tractable_target.claim: diffusion_conditioning is 36.9462 % of the model over 26 tensors -- but FOUR of those tensors are 33.9354 % on their own, 91.85 % of the section. The remaining 22 tensors are 3.0107 % of the model between them.
the_tractable_target.scale: 1,985 scalars. 0.000539 % of the model's parameters. A third of the gradient.
the_tractable_target.why_it_matters: the campaign's largest open item has been diffusion_conditioning, blocked on moving device_gradient.py's walked boundary. At 1,985 scalars the dominant part of it does not need the full module arm to be checked -- four float64 vectors can be compared exhaustively, entry by entry, on a host.

is_this_just_a_dimension_artifact: partly, but not mostly. Per-entry rms: 5.272e-02 for the heaviest LayerNorm bias (384 entries) against 2.661e-03 for the heaviest matrix in the top twelve (49,152 entries) -- the LayerNorm entries are individually ~20x larger, and there are ~128x fewer of them. Both effects are real and they compound in the same direction. Mechanically this is expected: a LayerNorm gain/bias gradient is a sum over every token and every sample of the normalized activation, so it accumulates a very large number of terms into a short vector, while a matrix gradient is an outer product spread across many entries.
does_the_share_matter: for this campaign's question, yes. The question is whether our gradient IS the reference gradient -- a statement about one vector in parameter space -- so the squared-norm share is the right denominator, and it is also what a global grad-norm clip sees. It is NOT the right denominator for per-parameter-adaptive optimisers: Adam divides each coordinate by its own second moment, which removes most of this concentration from the actual step. A parity failure concentrated in these vectors would show up loudly in a gradient-norm comparison and quietly in an Adam trajectory. Both facts should be stated whenever this table is quoted.
what_this_does_not_establish: mass is not error. Nothing here says the LayerNorm gradients are where our port is wrong -- no arm has been run at this cut. It says where a given amount of error costs most, and therefore which arm is worth building next. One batch (batch_step003, 5nw3, 56 real tokens), one r = 0 step; the stability of these shares across batches is unmeasured.
provenance: measured 2026-09-20 pass 151 on tt-quietbox2, torch.load + per-tensor float64 sum-of-squares, /home/ttuser/tt-bio-dev/env/bin/python, no Tenstorrent device opened, nice -n 15 alongside the live of3t-auxheads row.

concentration.what_it_means_for_the_campaigns_bar: the 2.0e-02 median-over-tensors bar is evaluated on the half of the gradient that holds one part in 1,740 of its mass. It is a good per-tensor safety net and it cannot be the headline. Filed as PROTOCOL A23 and D51.

a14_threshold_gap.note: A14 excludes only the first row. The other 96 tensors are nonzero by norm and zero by mass. The fix is to weight by mass, not to raise the epsilon.

aux_heads_is_one_tensor.note: measured, not rounded: the distogram linear weight is 100.0000 % of aux_heads' gradient mass. A median over the section's 244 tensors is a median over 243 numbers with no mass behind them. It is also one of the eight tensors the reference's finite-difference axis validated directly (rel 1.387e-05), so a disagreement found on it is unambiguously ours.
